{{< include ../_plot-setup.qmd >}}

Plot the model before interpreting its statistics: check the response shape,
event timing, column structure, correlations, and contrast weights. These
helpers return Matplotlib figures. For the fitted-model plots, see the
[figure gallery](plot-gallery.qmd).

On narrow screens, scroll plots horizontally to read their labels. Select a
plot for the complete view.

## Follow events into regressors

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

import fmrimod as fm
from fmrimod.hrf import get_hrf
from fmrimod.plotting import plot_hrf, plot_hrfs
from fmrimod.spec import compile as compile_spec
from fmrimod.spec import hrf
from fmrimod.visualization import (
    correlation_map,
    design_correlations,
    design_map,
    plot_event_model,
    plot_sampling_frame,
)

events = pd.DataFrame({
    "onset": [0.0, 10.0, 20.0, 30.0],
    "condition": ["face", "scene", "face", "scene"],
    "duration": 2.0,
})
sampling = fm.SamplingFrame(blocklens=60, TR=1.0)
event_model, _ = compile_spec(hrf("condition", basis="spmg1"), data=events, sampling_frame=sampling)
```

```{python}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-cap: "Realized face and scene regressors on the acquisition grid, one row per condition. Ticks under each row mark that condition's onsets and bars their 2 s durations, so each response can be traced to its event."
#| fig-alt: "Two stacked line charts, face above scene, each showing two hemodynamic responses over sixty seconds with onset ticks underneath."
fig = plot_event_model(event_model, figsize=(7, 3.2))
plt.show()
```

`style="overlay"` puts every regressor on one amplitude axis instead, and
`style="heatmap"` (chosen automatically for large designs such as
trialwise models) draws one raster row per regressor.

## View the design as a matrix

`design_map()` draws the matrix itself, one row per scan and one column per
regressor, the way SPM shows it. Each column is divided by its largest
absolute value so columns in different units share one colour scale; the
grey bars underneath keep the real magnitudes visible, and a column that is
nearly flat next to the rest of its term is marked in orange.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 6.6
#| fig-cap: "The face and scene columns of the design matrix, scans running downward. Bars under the matrix compare each column's peak with the largest in its term."
#| fig-alt: "Heatmap with two columns, face and scene, showing alternating red bands where each condition's responses occur, with a colour bar below."
fig = design_map(event_model)
plt.show()
```

The same call works on a `BaselineModel`, where drift and intercept columns
are grouped by run, and on a full `FmriModel`.

## Inspect column correlations

`correlation_map()` shows every pair of regressors once, as the lower
triangle of the correlation matrix. Pairs at or above `|r| = 0.5` are
outlined, and the diagonal carries each column's variance inflation factor
(VIF), which catches collinearity that no single pair reveals; VIFs of 5 or
more turn orange.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Pairwise correlation and diagonal VIF values for the alternating face and scene regressors. Inspect these alongside numerical rank; pairwise correlations alone do not establish estimability."
#| fig-alt: "A single shaded cell giving the face-scene correlation, with the variance inflation factor of each regressor on the diagonal."
fig = correlation_map(event_model)
plt.show()
```

The numbers are available without a plot:

```{python}
design_correlations(event_model).round(2)
```

## Check contrast weights

`plot_contrasts()` lays each contrast out as a row of weights over the same
columns. Two margin columns check every row: `sum w` (a non-zero sum, in
orange, means the contrast is not a pure comparison) and `SE ×σ`, the
standard error the design gives the contrast per unit of noise; lower is
better. An `EventModel` with contrasts on its terms can be passed directly;
here the weights are given by hand, with the model supplying the design.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-cap: "A face-versus-scene comparison and the face effect alone. The comparison sums to zero; the single-condition contrast does not."
#| fig-alt: "Two rows of contrast weights over the face and scene columns, with sum and standard-error columns at the right."
from fmrimod.contrast import plot_contrasts

fig = plot_contrasts(
    {"face_vs_scene": [1, -1], "face": [1, 0]},
    labels=["face", "scene"],
    design=event_model,
)
plt.show()
```

## Check the acquisition grid

The sampling-frame plot is useful when a model has multiple runs or unusual
TRs. It reads the timing object already used by design construction. Here
three runs, one of them shorter: the odd run is set in bold and the caption
says why, and passing the event table draws each onset under its run, so a
run without events or with an empty tail stands out.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 7.6
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-cap: "Three runs on one time axis. The third run is 20 scans short (bold), and the ticks under each bar show where the events fall."
#| fig-alt: "Three horizontal bars, one per run, laid end to end on a time axis, with small onset ticks beneath each bar."
runs = fm.SamplingFrame(blocklens=[60, 60, 40], TR=1.0)
run_events = pd.DataFrame({
    "onset": [5.0, 20.0, 40.0, 8.0, 30.0, 50.0, 12.0],
    "run": [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3],
})
fig = plot_sampling_frame(runs, events=run_events)
plt.show()
```

`style="grid"` shows each run's scans as cells on a within-run axis instead,
and `style="lane"` packs the runs into one annotated row.

## Inspect baseline terms

The baseline model holds the drift, intercept and nuisance columns. Its
plot draws every time-varying term on the shared time axis, one panel per
term, and lists the constant terms (here the run intercepts) in the caption,
together with the high-pass period the drift basis roughly corresponds to.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 7.6
#| fig-height: 4.0
#| fig-cap: "Cubic polynomial drift, three columns per run. Each run gets its own copy, and no line crosses a run boundary."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of three polynomial drift curves repeated in each of three runs, with a key at the right edge."
baseline = fm.baseline_model(basis="poly", degree=3, sframe=runs)
fig = baseline.plot()
plt.show()
```

`design_map(baseline)` and `correlation_map(baseline)` show the same columns
as a matrix and as within-run correlations.

## Inspect the HRF basis

The `fmrimod.plotting` module covers HRF and regressor plots. Use it to inspect
an HRF object before it is convolved into a design. Each function returns a
matplotlib `Figure`.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "Normalized SPM canonical HRF: a positive peak followed by a smaller undershoot. This is the response shape used by the design above."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of the normalized SPM canonical hemodynamic response, rising to one positive peak near five seconds, annotated with the peak time, and falling through a shallow undershoot."
fig = plot_hrf(get_hrf("spmg1"), normalize=True)
plt.show()
```

A basis set expands to one curve per basis function, labelled at its peak, so
you can see what each column of a multi-basis term models.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-cap: "The SPMG3 basis: the canonical response with its temporal and dispersion derivatives, which absorb small shifts in latency and width."
#| fig-alt: "Three curves labelled canonical, temporal deriv. and dispersion deriv.; the derivatives oscillate around zero within the canonical response's time window."
fig = plot_hrfs(get_hrf("spmg3"))
plt.show()
```
